questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: Amblyopia is best defined as:
options: Reduced vision in a structurally normal eye due to abnormal visual development
Loss of vision from retinal disease
questions.concept: Amblyopia results from form deprivation, strabismus or anisometropia during the critical period. Treatment by correcting refraction and occluding the better eye is effective only if started early, usually before 7 to 8 years.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: The Hirschberg corneal reflex test is used to:
options: Estimate the angle of deviation in squint
questions.concept: A torch reflex displaced from the pupil centre estimates deviation, with each millimetre corresponding to about 7 degrees. The cover-uncover test distinguishes manifest tropia from latent phoria.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) indicates:
options: Asymmetric optic nerve or extensive retinal disease
questions.concept: On swinging the torch, the affected pupil dilates because its afferent input is weaker. It is a purely afferent sign, so it never occurs with media opacities such as cataract, and is a key sign in optic neuritis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: A lesion at the optic chiasm characteristically produces:
questions.concept: Decussating nasal retinal fibres carrying temporal fields are damaged, classically by a pituitary adenoma extending upward, beginning in the upper temporal quadrants. Lesions behind the chiasm cause homonymous defects.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: A right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing suggests a lesion of:
questions.concept: Macular sparing reflects dual blood supply of the occipital pole by middle and posterior cerebral arteries, so posterior cerebral artery infarction spares central vision. Congruity increases the more posterior the lesion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: An Argyll Robertson pupil is characterised by:
options: A small irregular pupil that accommodates but does not react to light
questions.concept: Classically associated with neurosyphilis, it shows light-near dissociation with bilateral small irregular pupils. The Adie tonic pupil is instead large with slow tonic near response and absent tendon reflexes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: Sixth cranial nerve palsy produces:
options: Failure of abduction with convergent squint and horizontal diplopia worse on looking to the affected side
questions.concept: The abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course and is vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure, making its palsy a false localising sign. The eye deviates inward from unopposed medial rectus action.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: Optic neuritis in a young woman with pain on eye movement and a central scotoma should prompt evaluation for:
questions.concept: Optic neuritis is often the presenting feature of multiple sclerosis, and MRI showing periventricular white matter lesions predicts conversion. Intravenous methylprednisolone speeds recovery but does not alter final acuity.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: Fourth cranial nerve palsy characteristically causes:
options: Vertical diplopia worse on looking down, with compensatory head tilt to the opposite side
questions.concept: Superior oblique palsy impairs depression in adduction, so patients tilt the head away from the affected side (positive Bielschowsky test) and struggle going downstairs or reading.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Squint, amblyopia & neuro-ophthalmology (optic nerve, pupil, fields)
questions.stem: Pseudosquint in an Indian child is most often due to:
options: Prominent epicanthal folds giving an appearance of esotropia with normal corneal reflexes
questions.concept: Epicanthal folds obscure the nasal sclera creating an illusion of convergent squint, but corneal reflexes are symmetrical and cover test is normal. Any true squint after 6 months of age requires prompt referral.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: The immediate first aid for a chemical burn of the eye is:
options: Copious irrigation with clean water or saline before any other assessment
questions.concept: Immediate prolonged irrigation is the single most important determinant of outcome and must precede history-taking and acuity measurement. Alkali burns penetrate deeper by saponification and are more damaging than acids.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: A blowout fracture of the orbital floor characteristically causes:
options: Diplopia on upgaze with enophthalmos and infraorbital anaesthesia
questions.concept: Entrapment of inferior rectus and orbital fat in the maxillary sinus restricts elevation, and infraorbital nerve injury causes cheek numbness. CT shows the teardrop sign of herniated contents.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Hyphaema after blunt ocular trauma is managed by:
options: Rest with head elevation, monitoring intraocular pressure, and avoiding aspirin
questions.concept: Most hyphaemas resorb spontaneously; the risks are secondary rebleeding around days 3 to 5, raised intraocular pressure and corneal blood staining. Aspirin and NSAIDs are avoided as they promote rebleeding.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Retrobulbar haemorrhage after injury or block presents with:
options: Proptosis, tense orbit, raised intraocular pressure and threatened vision requiring urgent canthotomy
questions.concept: This orbital compartment syndrome compromises the optic nerve blood supply within minutes, requiring immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis at the bedside rather than transfer for imaging.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: An intraocular foreign body of iron left in the eye causes:
options: Siderosis bulbi with rusty deposits, cataract and retinal degeneration
questions.concept: Iron dissociates causing siderosis with heterochromia, pupillary mydriasis, cataract and pigmentary retinopathy; copper causes chalcosis with a sunflower cataract and Kayser-Fleischer-like ring. Both need removal.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Topical timolol is contraindicated in:
questions.concept: Even topical beta blockers are systemically absorbed through the nasolacrimal duct, precipitating bronchospasm and bradycardia. Punctal occlusion reduces absorption; prostaglandin analogues are safer alternatives.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Atropine as a cycloplegic is preferred in children for refraction because it:
options: Produces complete cycloplegia, essential when accommodation is strong
questions.concept: Children have powerful accommodation that masks hypermetropia, so full cycloplegia with atropine ointment is used under 5 years. Systemic toxicity causes flushing, fever, dry mouth and delirium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Under the National Programme for Control of Blindness, blindness in India is defined as presenting visual acuity in the better eye of less than:
questions.concept: India revised its definition to below 3/60 to align with WHO, from the earlier 6/60 criterion. Cataract remains the leading cause of blindness, followed by refractive error, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: The commonest cause of blindness in India is:
questions.concept: Cataract accounts for the majority of blindness and is reversible by surgery, which is why the national programme emphasises cataract surgical rate and intraocular lens implantation. Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of visual impairment.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.topic: Ocular trauma, orbit, ocular pharmacology & blindness control
questions.stem: Vision 2020: The Right to Sight targets which priority conditions?
options: Cataract, refractive error, childhood blindness, trachoma, onchocerciasis and glaucoma
questions.concept: The global initiative targets avoidable blindness through disease control, human resource development and infrastructure. In India cataract, refractive error, childhood blindness and glaucoma are the operational priorities.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: The earliest and most reliable clinical sign of acute compartment syndrome is:
options: Pain out of proportion to injury, worsened by passive stretch of the compartment muscles
questions.concept: Pulselessness and paralysis are late signs occurring after irreversible muscle necrosis. Pain on passive stretch with a tense swollen compartment demands immediate fasciotomy; a normal pulse never excludes the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Volkmann ischaemic contracture most classically follows:
options: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a child
questions.concept: Brachial artery injury or a tight cast causes forearm compartment ischaemia, and subsequent fibrosis produces flexion contracture of the fingers that relaxes on wrist flexion. Early recognition and fasciotomy prevent it.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Fat embolism syndrome after a long bone fracture typically presents:
options: 24 to 72 hours after injury with hypoxia, confusion and petechiae
questions.concept: The classic triad of respiratory distress, neurological change and a petechial rash over the axilla, conjunctiva and upper chest appears after a latent interval. Management is supportive with oxygen and early fracture fixation.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Delayed union differs from non-union in that:
options: Union is slower than expected but the healing process is still ongoing
questions.concept: Non-union shows a sclerosed sealed medullary canal with persistent mobility and no radiological progression over three months, requiring bone grafting and stable fixation; delayed union may still unite with time and protection.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Avascular necrosis is a particular risk after fracture of the:
questions.concept: These bones have a retrograde blood supply entering distally, so a proximal fracture interrupts perfusion of the proximal fragment. This is why undisplaced scaphoid fractures are immobilised even with a normal initial radiograph.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: A greenstick fracture is characteristic of children because:
options: Their bone is soft with a thick periosteum, so it bends and breaks on one cortex only
questions.concept: Paediatric bone is more porous and elastic with a thick osteogenic periosteum, giving incomplete fractures, rapid healing and considerable remodelling potential, but also physeal injuries with growth disturbance.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Fractures in Children

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: An open (compound) fracture requires:
options: Urgent wound debridement, antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis with fracture stabilisation
questions.concept: The Gustilo-Anderson classification grades severity. Early antibiotics, thorough debridement and stabilisation reduce infection, which is the principal complication; primary closure is avoided in contaminated wounds.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: The Salter-Harris classification describes:
options: Physeal (growth plate) injuries in children, with higher types carrying greater growth arrest risk
questions.concept: Type I is through the physis, II extends into metaphysis (commonest), III into epiphysis, IV crosses both, and V is a crush injury with the worst prognosis for growth arrest and deformity.
questions.reference: Maheshwari Essential Orthopaedics 6e, Fractures in Children

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Compartment pressure measurement supports fasciotomy when the delta pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) is:
questions.concept: A delta pressure below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate perfusion. Measurement supports but never replaces clinical judgement, and in a convincing clinical picture fasciotomy should not await manometry.

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.topic: Fracture principles, complications & compartment syndrome
questions.stem: Complex regional pain syndrome (Sudeck atrophy) after a fracture presents with:
options: Disproportionate burning pain, swelling, vasomotor changes and patchy osteopenia
questions.concept: Sympathetically mediated pain with allodynia, trophic skin changes and spotty osteoporosis follows apparently minor injury, classically after Colles fracture. Early mobilisation, physiotherapy and analgesia are the mainstay.
